Fast, fair calibration

Source: performance.md

This guide covers three changes made for benchmarking PDM against LSTM models across many basins: multi-start calibration, a compiled simulation engine, and a guard on the Smith groundwater solver. Read it before planning a large calibration run.

The short version: a 29-year, 15-minute calibration of 60 basins with 20 starts each now takes about a day on 16 cores, down from about 7,500 hours on 64 cores in pure R. Your code does not change; the speed comes automatically for the default model.

Why this matters

A benchmark is only fair if both models are calibrated properly. calibrate_pdm() uses L-BFGS-B, a local optimiser. From a single starting point it can settle in a local optimum and under-calibrate PDM, which would flatter the model it is compared with. Multi-start calibration addresses that. Running many starts over many basins at 15-minute resolution was not feasible in R, which is why the compiled engine came next.

Quick start

Daily data

library(pdmS7)

config <- pdm_presets("standard")
config$dt <- 24          # model interval in hours: 24 for daily data
config$area_km2 <- 100   # your catchment area

# forcing: data.frame with rain and pet in mm per interval
# observed: discharge in m3/s, aligned to the forcing rows
fit <- calibrate_pdm(
  config, forcing, observed,
  lower = c(fc = 0.5, recharge.kg = 5, groundwater.kb = 5000),
  upper = c(fc = 2, recharge.kg = 60, groundwater.kb = 20000),
  warmup = 365, objective = "nse",
  starts = 20L, seed = 42
)

fit$parameters      # best parameter set
fit$objective       # best objective (1 - NSE here)
fit$start_results   # one row per start

15-minute data

Set dt to 0.25 hours. Everything else is the same.

config <- pdm_presets("standard")
config$dt <- 0.25
config$area_km2 <- 100

fit <- calibrate_pdm(
  config, forcing, observed,
  lower = c(fc = 0.5, recharge.kg = 5, groundwater.kb = 5000),
  upper = c(fc = 2, recharge.kg = 60, groundwater.kb = 20000),
  warmup = 35064, objective = "nse",   # one year of 15-minute steps
  starts = 20L, seed = 42
)

For a plain simulation, sim_pdm() takes the interval in minutes:

out <- sim_pdm(forcing$rain, forcing$pet, config, timestep_min = 15L)

Multi-start calibration

How it works

  1. Each parameter is rescaled to the unit interval between its lower and upper bound, so parameters with very different units are treated evenly.
  2. Start 1 is always the parameter values already in config. The remaining starts - 1 starting points are drawn uniformly at random inside the bounds.
  3. L-BFGS-B runs from every start, with the same control settings.
  4. The start with the lowest objective wins. Its parameters, configuration and model are returned, exactly as a single-start run returns them.

Because start 1 is the configured point, the best of several starts can never be worse than a single start from the same configuration.

Arguments

Argument Default Meaning
starts 1L Number of starts. 1L runs the same single optimisation as earlier versions.
seed NULL Seeds the random starting points, so a run can be repeated. Your session’s random number state is restored afterwards. Ignored when starts is 1.

All other arguments are unchanged: lower, upper, warmup, objective (rmse, nse or log_rmse), flow (q_m3s or q_end_m3s), log_offset, control and soil_fraction.

What comes back

The result has the same fields as before, describing the best start, plus start_results:

Column Meaning
start Start number. 1 is the configured point.
objective Final objective for that start, on the scale named by objective_name (for nse it is 1 - NSE). 1e+30 means no valid evaluation.
convergence The stats::optim code. 0 is normal convergence; 1 means the iteration limit was reached; 51 and 52 are L-BFGS-B warnings and stops, usually a line search that could make no further progress.
evaluations Number of model simulations used by that start, including the gradient calls optim leaves out of its own count.
best TRUE for the start that was returned.
one column per parameter The fitted value from that start. Always within the bounds.

Reading the results

  • Several starts reaching the same objective suggests the optimum is well defined.
  • A wide spread of objectives means the surface has local optima, and a single start would have been unreliable.
  • The same objective from different parameter values points to equifinality: the data cannot separate those parameters. Narrow the bounds or fix one of them.
  • convergence of 1 means the start hit maxit. Raise control = list(maxit = ...) if the best start shows it.
  • convergence of 51 or 52 often means the optimiser could not improve further, for example on a flat surface or at a perfect fit. Check the objective before treating it as a failure.

How many starts?

Twenty is a cautious default, not a rule. Run a pilot on three to five representative basins with 20 starts, then check where the best objective first appears.

inst/examples/pilot_calibration.R does this for you. It reads one CSV per basin, calibrates the basins in parallel, and reports for each basin the start that first reached the best objective, the spread across starts, convergence and any parameter on a bound. It then budgets the full run from the measured cost. PILOT_SYNTHETIC=1 gives a dry run on synthetic basins. Run the pilot with the same maxit as the full run, because evaluation counts, and so the budget, depend on it. To check a single fit by hand:

tab <- fit$start_results
data.frame(start = tab$start, objective = tab$objective, best_so_far = cummin(tab$objective))

If the best value is usually reached within the first five starts, five is enough, and the full run costs a quarter as much.

Reproducibility

With a fixed seed, the same inputs give the same result every time. Use a different seed per basin when running in parallel, so the basins do not share starting points by accident:

seed = 1000L + basin_index

Running basins in parallel

Parallelism is left to the caller. Run one basin per worker; each worker runs its starts in sequence. This works on Windows as well as Linux:

library(parallel)

cl <- makeCluster(detectCores() - 1L)
clusterEvalQ(cl, library(pdmS7))
clusterExport(cl, c("basins", "lower", "upper"))

fits <- parLapply(cl, seq_along(basins), function(i) {
  b <- basins[[i]]
  calibrate_pdm(
    b$config, b$forcing, b$observed, lower, upper,
    warmup = b$warmup, objective = "nse",
    starts = 20L, seed = 1000L + i
  )
})
stopCluster(cl)

Here basins is a list with one entry per catchment, each holding config, forcing, observed and warmup.

The compiled engine

What it does

Each time step of PDM is a few dozen arithmetic operations. In R, the work around them cost far more: building S7 objects, validating them, and creating a one-row data.table at every step. A profile put the groundwater maths itself at under 10 per cent of the run time.

The compiled engine runs the whole time loop in C. It covers:

  • capacity distribution: Pareto, rectangular, exponential, triangular or lognormal;
  • recharge: standard, split or demand;
  • surface and groundwater routes, chosen independently: two-store cascade, power-law store (linear, quadratic, cubic or any exponent, with either solver) or exponential store.

That is every PDM component in the package, so run_pdm() always uses the compiled loop unless options(pdmS7.engine = "r") is set. The PACK snowpack (sim_pack(), and so sim_snow_pdm()) is compiled too, about 540 times faster than its R loop. You do not choose; it happens automatically. sim_pdm() and calibrate_pdm() both go through run_pdm(), so they speed up too.

Is the output the same?

Yes, to rounding. The C code repeats the R arithmetic in the same order, so the two engines agree to the last one or two decimal places of a double, around 1e-15 relative. On R 4.3 they are bit-identical. On R 4.5 and 4.6 they differ in the last place, because those versions changed how R’s own sum() and ^ round. tests/testthat/test-engine.R compares every output column, the final state and the water balance between the two engines across eight model configurations, restarts and timestamped forcing, and requires each to agree within 1e-12 of its own magnitude.

A calibration amplifies these differences slightly: optimised parameters agree to about 1e-13 relative. That is far below any meaningful parameter uncertainty.

To run the original R loop, for checking or debugging:

options(pdmS7.engine = "r")     # R loop
options(pdmS7.engine = "auto")  # back to the default

The calibration path

During calibration only the scored flow series is needed. calibrate_pdm() uses an internal path that returns just that series and skips the 24-column flux table. At 15 minutes this halves the time per evaluation. The values are the same as run_pdm() would give.

Measured speed

On a 4-core Xeon at 2.1 GHz with R 4.3.3:

Run Time per simulation
10,600 daily steps, R loop 23.5 s
10,600 daily steps, compiled 0.055 s
29 years of 15-minute steps, compiled 2.5 s
29 years of 15-minute steps, compiled, calibration path 1.2 s

A full daily calibration with three parameters took 60 s and 938 evaluations. The R loop would have needed about six hours. Full details are in the timing report.

Installing

The package now contains compiled code: the model core in C and a thin C++ wrapper for R. So building from source needs a compiler. On Windows that means Rtools matched to your R version; on macOS, the Xcode command line tools; on Linux, the usual build tools. The cpp11 package is needed at build time only; nothing extra is loaded when the package runs.

install.packages("cpp11")
install.packages("pdmS7_0.3.1.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")

Choosing a groundwater solver

Cubic groundwater routing has two solvers:

  • adaptive (the default): step-doubling Runge-Kutta. Accurate at every time step tested.
  • smith: a closed-form approximation, about a quarter faster.

Smith’s error grows with the square of the time step, and is worse for faster stores (smaller kb). Maximum error as a percentage of peak flow:

Step kb 1,000 kb 10,000 kb 50,000
15 minutes 0.06 0.02 0.007
1 hour 1.0 0.26 0.11
3 hours 5.5 2.2 1.0
24 hours 100 100 62

Use adaptive unless you need the last quarter of speed at a 15-minute step. Never use Smith for daily data. pdm_model() warns, once per R session, when Smith is combined with a step above 1 hour. Only the paper_cubic preset selects Smith; every other preset uses adaptive. inst/benchmarks/smith_step_error.R reproduces the table.

Budgeting a large run

Total time is:

basins x starts x evaluations per start x seconds per evaluation / cores

For 60 basins, 20 starts and 938 evaluations per start, that gives:

Cores Daily 15-minute
4 5.0 hours 92 hours
16 1.2 hours 23 hours
64 0.3 hours 5.8 hours

The 15-minute figures assume the same number of evaluations as the daily test. Real basins will differ. Before booking compute, run the pilot described above and use the evaluation counts from its start_results.

Recommended workflow

  1. Prepare the forcing. Rain and PET in mm per interval, discharge in m3/s, all on the same intervals. Set config$dt to the interval in hours.
  2. Choose the warm-up. A year is a reasonable start. Warm-up steps are simulated but not scored.
  3. Set bounds. Keep them physically plausible. Bounds that are too wide waste evaluations; bounds that are too narrow can exclude the optimum.
  4. Pilot. Three to five basins, 20 starts, fixed seeds. Check the spread in start_results and how many starts were needed.
  5. Run. All basins in parallel, one basin per worker, a distinct seed per basin.
  6. Check. For each basin, look at convergence, the spread of objectives, and whether any fitted parameter sits on a bound.
  7. Validate. Score the calibrated model on an independent period before comparing it with the LSTM.

Limitations

  • Multi-start calibration reduces the risk of a local optimum; it does not guarantee the global one.
  • Uniform random starts cover the parameter space less evenly than a space-filling design such as a Latin hypercube. With 20 starts and three or four parameters this rarely matters.
  • Evaluation counts depend on the basin, the objective, the bounds and the number of parameters.

For maintainers: extending the engine

The model arithmetic lives in src/pdm_core.c, plain C99 behind the interface in src/pdm_core.h. It has no R dependency, so other languages can call it; tools/core/README.md explains how. src/pdm_engine.cpp is only the R wrapper. The PACK snowpack is in the core too.

To port another component:

  1. Add its step to src/pdm_core.c, mirroring the R expression in the same evaluation order. Use rpow() for ^ and the long-double helpers for sum().
  2. Add its parameters to pdm_params in src/pdm_core.h, with validation rules no stricter than the S7 validator, and raise PDM_CORE_ABI_VERSION. Other languages’ bindings must follow the new layout.
  3. Pass its parameters through .engine_run() in R/engine.R and src/pdm_engine.cpp.
  4. Add its class to .engine_supported(). Matching is by exact class, so subclasses stay on the R loop until they are added deliberately.
  5. Add a configuration using it to engine_models() in tests/testthat/test-engine.R, and a case to inst/golden/generate_golden.R. Regenerate the golden files and review the diff.
  6. Run cpp11::cpp_register() if a function signature changed, then roxygen2::roxygenise().

Any change to the model equations in R must be repeated in C. The equivalence and golden tests will fail until both agree.
